characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 17Al alloy aged at 625 °C for 10 h the average Vickers hardness is 870.5 ± 24.9 HV; the as-solutionised 17Al baseline is 259.8 ± 1.5 HV.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Load 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times and averaged
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure Vickers hardness of the solution-treated and aged Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steel samples

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: ZEISS Sigma 300 SEM operated at 5 kV
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 17Al alloy, increased Al content slows β-Mn precipitation kinetics at low temperatures; at 600 °C and above the α matrix almost fully transformed to β-Mn after 1 h, with dense fine dot-like precipitates within the transformed β-Mn.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Electrolytically polished samples (10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol); 50 µm main-field and 2-10 µm inset scale bars
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify the precipitation of secondary phases such as α-Mn and β-Mn in aged samples

characterization_methods.key_findings: Solution-treated alloys are single-phase α (BCC); after aging at high temperature the α transforms to β-Mn with new BCC and FCC precipitates (Fig. 5: 17Al at 575 °C/6 h and 650 °C/10 h).
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Scanning step size 1.5 μm for low magnification and 0.05 μm for high magnification
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine constituent phases and grain structure of solution-treated and aged alloys

characterization_methods.key_findings: Both α-Mn and β-Mn diffraction peaks are found in the selected partially-transformed samples (including 17Al at 575 °C/1 h), together with α/D0₃, indicating α-Mn and β-Mn co-precipitate before the α matrix fully transforms to β-Mn.
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify phase compositions of the alloys after aging

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: FEI Talos F200X microscope equipped with an EDS detector, operated at 200 kV
characterization_methods.key_findings: Fine FCC Cu-rich particles containing FCC twins precipitate at β-Mn interfaces (characterized for 15Al at 600 °C/6 h and 17Al at 575 °C/6 h).
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: TEM foils mechanically ground to ~90 μm, punched to 3 mm diameter and ion thinned
characterization_methods.purpose: Elucidate the microstructures of the ultra-high hardness alloys and characterize fine precipitates and interfaces
characterization_methods.technique: Transmission electron microscopy (BF/DF imaging, SAED, HRTEM, EDS)

characterization_methods.key_findings: Average nanoindentation hardness of the hardest samples was 11.7 ± 0.4 GPa (15Al), 11.1 ± 0.6 GPa (17Al) and 10.4 ± 1.3 GPa (19Al); intrinsic β-Mn hardness 12.1 ± 0.3, 12.2 ± 0.1 and 12.5 ± 0.4 GPa respectively.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Indentation depth 200 nm; test points spaced 5 μm or more apart; mechanically polished samples
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure intrinsic hardness of β-Mn and of the precipitate phases in the hardest samples

defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Fine FCC particles at the β-Mn interfaces exhibit an FCC crystal structure with FCC twins frequently observed within the particles.

interfaces.interface_notes: The FCC Cu-rich phase is rich in Cu, depleted in Fe and Mn, and slightly poor in Al; the β-Mn is poor in Cu. Cu-rich phase forms because of the limited solubility of Cu in Fe-based alloys and the expulsion of Cu from β-Mn during precipitation/growth; the BCC phase forms at β-Mn interfaces due to enrichment of the BCC-stabilizing element Al around the interfaces.
interfaces.phase_evolution: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Alloy ingots with nominal composition Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (at.%) produced by melting high-purity (>99.9%) raw materials in a vacuum induction furnace under an argon atmosphere; referred to as 17Al according to its Al content.
Ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h.
Homogenized ingots hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.
processing_steps.reduction_ratio: rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Plates were cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ samples using electrical discharge machining for Vickers hardness measurements and microstructure characterizations.
Solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching; the solution-treated 17Al alloy had a single α (BCC) phase and a hardness of 259.8 ± 1.5 HV.
The solution-treated 17Al alloy was aged at 625 °C for 10 h, followed by water quenching; this is the defining process of the sample (state 625°C-10h).

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers hardness measured with a load of 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample repeatedly tested 5 times and the reported value is the average of 5 measurements.

structures.overall_structure: Single-phase α (body-centered cubic, BCC) matrix in the solution-treated (1100 °C/10 min + oil quench) 17Al alloy; the IPF map shows a dominant large green grain surrounded by blue, purple, cyan and orange neighbours and the phase map is uniformly red (α/BCC).

phases_present.morphology: fine precipitates within β-Mn, size comparable to FCC Cu-rich particles
fine particles at β-Mn interfaces, frequently containing FCC twins

precipitates.distribution: within β-Mn and at β-Mn interfaces

structures.overall_structure: After high-temperature aging (600 °C and above), the α matrix of the 17Al alloy had almost completely transformed into β-Mn within just 1 h; consequently the 625 °C/10 h state consists essentially of a β-Mn matrix with fine new BCC and FCC (Cu-rich) precipitates inside the β-Mn. The α→β-Mn transformation sequence is α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase.

unmapped_findings: For the 17Al alloy, the hardness contour plots show that the >900 HV region is a broad band roughly between 600 and 650 °C and an isolated island around 575-600 °C at ~5-9 h (Fig. 2b); the 625 °C and 650 °C rows reach ~813-878 HV and ~828-838 HV respectively and stay nearly flat across 1-10 h.

For the 17Al alloy the hardness increased gradually during low-temperature aging at 525 °C and 550 °C but failed to reach peak hardness; during aging at 575 °C and above the rate of hardness increase was accelerated while the maximum hardness value decreased (peak 924.9 HV at 575 °C/6 h).

The optimal aging temperature range for ultra-high hardness shifted to higher temperatures with increasing Al content (525-600 °C for 15Al, 550-600 °C for 17Al and 575-625 °C for 19Al); the 625 °C/10 h condition of this sample therefore lies at the upper end of the 17Al ultra-high-hardness window.

The fracture toughness K_IC of the ultra-hard Fe-Mn-Al-Cu alloys decreased with increasing Al content (8.6 MPa·m^1/2 for 15Al, 6.6 MPa·m^1/2 for 17Al and 3.5 MPa·m^1/2 for 19Al), with corresponding average crack lengths of 18 μm (15Al), 22 μm (17Al) and 35 μm (19Al); these values were measured on the peak-hardness samples (HV = 924.9 for 17Al at 575 °C/6 h), not on the 625 °C/10 h sample.

The increase in Al content slowed the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn, so the α→β-Mn transformation of the 17Al alloy completed only after 6 h at 550 °C (versus 3 h at 525 °C for 15Al); at 600 °C and above both 17Al and 19Al transformed after 1 h.
